title: Investigation of Widefield NV-Center Magnetic Imaging for Non-Destructive Materials Testing
authors: Niklas Mathesa, Marvin Feuerhelm, Simon Philipp, Ivan Soldatov, Philipp DÁstolfo, Peter Knittel, Thomas Straubb, Jan Jeske, Rüdiger Quay, Xavier Vidal
abstract: Due to progressing miniaturization, material fatigue is expected to gain importance on microscopic scales. Nevertheless, most non-destructive testing techniques are optimized for macroscopic scales. Therefore, new approaches applicable to miniaturized samples need to be explored. High spatial resolution imaging of a material's magnetic stray field enables sensitive detection of microstructural changes due to the local interplay of magnetic properties, strain, and defects. Up to now, this approach has rarely been used for materials testing since high-resolution magnetic sensing is traditionally challenging. Novel quantum sensing techniques offer the potential to close this gap. One of the most prominent quantum sensors, the nitrogen vacancy center in diamond, is investigated for non-destructive testing applications within the scope of this work. An experimental system based on a widefield sensing approach was developed to image magnetic stray field distributions within seconds to minutes over areas up to 1 x 1 $mm^2$. Magnetic sensitivities below 10 $μ$T/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ and a spatial resolution of 1-2 $μ$m were achieved. The technique offers high mechanical stability, which is crucial for non-destructive testing applications. Comparison with magneto-optical Kerr effect measurements showed that the magnetic field maps are strongly correlated with the material's surface domains while containing additional information from deeper inside the sample. Characteristic changes in the magnetic stray field distribution were detected in an electrical steel sample after cyclic loading. A potential marker for early fatigue damage was deduced from the splitting gradient distribution, while 2D Fourier transform analysis provided additional insight.
summary: This research presents a novel, widefield quantum sensing technique using NV centers in diamond to image magnetic stray fields for non-destructive testing. By achieving high spatial resolution and sensitivity, the method can detect subtle magnetic signatures associated with early-stage material fatigue and microstructural damage. This advances the application of quantum sensing from fundamental physics into practical materials engineering.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for non-destructive testing (NDT) techniques capable of imaging microstructural changes in miniaturized materials, particularly those related to fatigue damage.
main_result: A widefield NV-center magnetic imaging technique was developed, achieving high sensitivity and spatial resolution to detect characteristic magnetic stray field changes indicative of early fatigue damage in materials like electrical steel.
method: The authors developed and applied an experimental system using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond to image magnetic stray field distributions over macroscopic areas.
model_or_system: The physical system is the NV center in diamond, which acts as a quantum sensor whose spin state is sensitive to the local magnetic field ($\vec{B}$). The measurement relies on mapping the magnetic stray field distribution, which is influenced by the material's magnetic microstructure and defects.
key_observables: Magnetic stray field distribution, Zeeman splitting maps, and characteristic changes in the magnetic field pattern after cyclic loading.
important_parameters: Magnetic sensitivities below $10 \mu	ext{T}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$ and a spatial resolution of $1-2 \mu	ext{m}$.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes that material fatigue alters the magnetic microstructure (e.g., domain wall pinning) in a way that produces a measurable, localized change in the stray magnetic field.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physics of domain wall separation and pinning at defects, and the general setup for widefield sensing.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (NDT for small scales), introduces the quantum sensor (NV center), details the widefield experimental setup and achieved metrics, and demonstrates the application by detecting fatigue-related magnetic changes in test samples.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates a direct, applied use of quantum sensing (NV centers) to solve a complex condensed matter problem (material failure analysis), bridging quantum physics with industrial materials science.
